articles.title: BFP bet beats Lamitan vice mayor for Basilan 1st District parliament seat
articles.summary: The BFP's Rima Hassan clinches the race, after Lamitan City Mayor Roderick 'Oric' Furigay endorsed her party over the party of his nephew

blocks.text: Supporters of Rima Hassan/Facebook
The BFP's Rima Hassan clinches the race, after Lamitan City Mayor Roderick 'Oric' Furigay endorsed her party over the party of his nephew

MANILA, Philippines – Lamitan Councilor Rima Hasim Hassan tops the race for Basilan’s 1st District representative to the Bangsamoro Parliament, following the historic 2026 Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) elections.
She has obtained 21,933 votes, based on 95.40% of total election returns for the 2026 BARMM parliamentary elections as of Monday, September 14, 11:44 pm.

Her closest competitor was Lamitan City Vice Mayor Hegem Cabrera Furigay, who got 14,733 votes. He ran under the Bangsamoro Peoples Party, a relatively lesser known party led by former BARMM member of parliament Alzad Sattar.

Hegem did not receive the endorsement of his uncle and Lamitan City Mayor Roderick “Oric” Furigay. Oric instead joined 9 other Basilan mayors in endorsing Hassan’s party, the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP).
Coming in third for Basilan’s 1st District race was Moro Islamic Liberation Front commander Verjiv Flores Abdurahman of the United Justice Bangsamoro Party who received 4,491 votes.

Hassan would serve a special five-year transition term from October 30, 2026 to June 30, 2031. She will be one of the 32 district representatives making up 40% of the 80-seat Bangsamoro Parliament. – Rappler.com

articles.title: BFP, UBJP lead BARMM parliamentary party race – PPCRV
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) remained the top regional parliamentary political party (RPPP) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) remained the top regional parliamentary political party (RPPP) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections, the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) reported on Tuesday.
Based on the PPCRV’s unofficial parallel count as of 5:30 a.m., the BFP still led the region’s political party race with 652,227 votes (35.0 percent).

This was followed by UBJP with 604,968 votes (32.4 percent), then the BARMM Grand Coalition with 385,396 votes (20.7 percent), and the Bangsamoro Peoples’ Democratic Party, also known as the Rayaat Democratic Party, with 67,800 votes (3.6 percent).
The four parties met the RPPP’s 2.5 percent threshold to secure a seat in the 80-member parliament.

articles.title: BFP bet set to win Maguindanao del Norte 1st District BARMM seat
articles.summary: Prince Khalid Tomawis is the son of the late former Barira mayor Alexander Tomawis and former Buldon mayor Fatima Ruth Tomawis

blocks.text: Bangsamoro Federalist Party/Facebook
Prince Khalid Tomawis is the son of the late former Barira mayor Alexander Tomawis and former Buldon mayor Fatima Ruth Tomawis
COTABATO CITY, Philippines – Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) bet Prince Khalid Tomawis currently tops the Bangsamoro parliamentary electoral race in the 1st District of Maguindanao del Norte.

The province is the bailiwick of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), which is led by former acting Maguindanao del Norte governor and Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao interim Chief Minister Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua.

Tomawis has received 38,937 votes with 94.51% precincts reporting as of September 14, 10:59 pm. He is the son of the late former Barira mayor Alexander Tomawis and former Buldon mayor Fatima Ruth Tomawis.

The BFP bet’s closest competitor is Abdulkudos Pendatu Balitok, former base commander of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). He has obtained 16,816 votes so far, making it impossible to catch up given Tomawis’ lead.
Balitok ran under the banner of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party, the MILF’s political party. – Rappler.com

articles.title: QC RTC judge junks Sara Duterte's motion to inhibit from grave threats case
articles.summary: The Quezon City Regional Trial Court has denied the motion for inhibition or voluntary recusal filed by Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 8:30am Updated September 15, 2026 8:43am
The Quezon City Regional Trial Court has denied the motion for inhibition or voluntary recusal filed by Vice President Sara Duterte.
In an order dated September 14, QCRTC Branch 98 Presiding Judge Maria Angelica De Ramos said the motion lacks merit.

"All told, absent any clear and convincing evidence of actual bias, prejudgment, or an improper connection that reasonably calls the undersigned's impartiality into question, the undersigned sees no cogent reason for her to inhibit or recuse herself from hearing these cases," the document secured by GMA News read.
The motion was filed on September 10.
GMA News Online reached out to the camp of the Vice President for comment and will post it once available.
Duterte is facing three counts of grave threats in connection with remarks she made in an online press conference in 2024.

During the press conference, Duterte said she had already talked to someone to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then House Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.
The court issued the arrest warrant last Friday, and Duterte posted bail on Saturday.
The Vice President's arraignment was set on Monday, but it was postponed due to a motion filed by her camp. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte wealth case: The argument for examining Mans Carpio’s finances
articles.summary: The Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act says properties in the name of the spouse of a public official may be considered when determining their unexplained wealth

blocks.text: COMPLAINT. Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, arrives at the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office along with his legal counsel, to file a criminal complaint against BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr., AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, and members of the House Committee on Justice over alleged violations of banking privacy and data protection laws, on April 27, 2026.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act says properties in the name of the spouse of a public official may be considered when determining their unexplained wealth

items: Prosecutor Chel Diokno questioned the inclusion of properties owned by individuals related to government officials in investigations, referencing the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.

Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang explained that financial records of a public official's spouse can be scrutinized to prevent evasion from investigation into illegally acquired properties.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

It doesn’t take a genius to understand where prosecutor Chel Diokno was going when he asked former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang what the law says about property owned by people other than the government official being investigated.

“Under Section 8 of RA 3019 (Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act), the properties in the name of other persons, and even the spouse and the children, may be considered in determining whether the official has acquired properties,” Tang said during the 24th day of the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, September 14.
Diokno was trying to establish the need to look into the financial records not only of the Vice President, but also those of her husband Mans Carpio.

It’s been a months-long effort by the House that already placed certain lawmakers in a legal battle outside the impeachment court, with Carpio suing House justice committee officials for disclosing his private financial records in April.

That is why the public knew that the Vice President, according to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), had P6.7 billion in large and suspicious bank transaction records in the past two decades — because the number includes P2.9 billion in funds that flowed through Carpio’s own bank accounts.

blocks.caption: IN NUMBERS: What impeachment hearings unveiled about Sara Duterte’s wealth

blocks.text: Carpio’s legal counsel had cited various laws that were supposedly violated when the House hearing released the AMLC report, including the Anti-Money Laundering Act, the Bank Secrecy Law, and the Data Privacy Act.
Quezon City prosecutors recently junked Carpio’s complaint, but only for lack of jurisdiction.
Tang also cited Philippines v Rabusa, a 2022 Supreme Court case involving a forfeiture proceeding filed by the government to recover alleged ill-gotten wealth by a military officer and his family.
In that ruling, the Court asserted that the inquiry should understandably extend to the spouse and dependents of AFP officer Rabusa.

“Such pervasiveness of the inquiry is clearly warranted, if only to prevent persons in government whoillegally acquire property from evading investigation by simply placing property in the possession of or in the name of other persons,” the decision reads.

The same resolution cited the 1990 Supreme Court ruling, Mellon Bank, N.A. v. Magsino, which emphasized that looking into the whereabouts of illegally acquired funds requires examining bank records “in the name of persons other than the one responsible for the illegal acquisition.”
Diokno’s direct examination also prompted Tang to explain that public officials’ SALN should include assets and business interests of their spouses.
Tang provided one exception, supported by the the 2019 Supreme Court ruling, Abid-Babano v Executive Secretary.
“If the spouses had a complete separation of property before the marriage, then the property of the spouse need not to be included in the official’s SALN,” Tang said.
Diokno quipped that a prenuptial agreement or a judicial separation of properties during marriage could therefore allow public officials to exclude their spouse’s assets from their SALNs.
But who is liable if the spouse does not make the declaration in the public official’s SALN?

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte wealth case: The argument for examining Mans Carpio’s finances

blocks.text: “Only the public official,” Tang said. “It’s only the government official who is required to file a SALN, and that public official is required to include the assets of her spouse.”
If a public official is proven to have acquired unexplained wealth during his or her term in office, he or she can be dismissed from office, based on RA 3019. – Rappler.com

articles.title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump's bid to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of November midterms
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail…

image.caption: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday against having the U.S. Postal Service restrict mail-in ballots. (Erin Scott/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail ahead ‌of November's midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
8 states conduct elections entirely by mail, while all 50 allow it in some form

The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to U.S. President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail ahead ‌of November's midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

The justices denied the Justice Department's request to lift a ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston that blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing the measure while legal challenges by states and voting-rights groups proceed. The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.
"The government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to ​the District Court's preliminary injunction," the court said in its brief, one-paragraph order.

Justice Samuel Alito, ​joined by fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented from Monday's decision, comparing some of the challengers' claims to a "Hail Mary pass" that is "unlikely to be successfully completed," using a football analogy.
"The Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail," Alito added.
Mail-in restrictions would likely benefit Republicans
No other justice dissented publicly. ​The court has a 6-3 conservative majority.

Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to benefit Republicans, given that Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according ​to various surveys.

Under ⁠the new rule, states must provide ⁠lists of mail ballot recipients to the Postal Service and use agency-approved outgoing and ‌return ballot envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes. The Postal Service could then refuse to send out ballots that do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not appear on the lists.

Critics have said the plan could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots as the November 3 midterm vote approaches and cause chaos, given imminent plans by many states to ⁠send out mail ballots to eligible voters.

Talwani imposed ​an injunction on Sept. 4 blocking the rule, finding that it likely violated the U.S. Constitution, under which states administer elections. Talwani also said it would be impossible for the states to comply given the ⁠rapidly approaching midterms.
Another federal judge, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., also ruled against the new rule on Sunday.
'Testing the limits' of power
Sophia Lin Lakin, voting rights project director at the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent some of the challengers to the USPS rule, welcomed Monday's decision.

"This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules ‌governing our elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don't suit the president's agenda. But the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to set the rules for federal elections — not the president, and not the Postal Service," she said.

"Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law and the American people looking to exercise their constitutional right to vote," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, whose state led one of the lawsuits against the rule.
"Trump's attacks on democracy these last 20 months ​have been nothing short of un-American."
Trump himself often votes by mail

Trump signed his executive order targeting mail-in ballots after years of casting doubt on their security, though he often votes by mail himself. Trump has made false claims of widespread fraud ‌in U.S. elections, including claims that fraud contributed to his 2020 loss to former Democratic president Joe Biden.
The administration, in a Sept. 6 emergency request, urged the Supreme Court to allow it to implement an "important federal policy to protect the mails from being used to commit voter fraud."
The truth behind Trump’s push to ban mail-in voting | About That

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston refused last Thursday to put Talwani's order on hold. The 1st Circuit said that the rule "will ⁠likely result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal — if any — gains in combating voter fraud."

Nichols granted ⁠a request ⁠from the Democratic Party and groups including the NAACP for ​a preliminary injunction blocking the rule. Nichols wrote that the rule could make it harder for some people to vote by mail and that it exceeded ​the Postal Service's authority.
"No statute grants the Postal ⁠Service the power to issue key parts of the rule," Nichols wrote.
All 50 states allow for some form of mail-in voting. Of those, 29 states allow voters to request mail ballots without providing a reason, and eight conduct their elections entirely by mail.

The battle over mail ballots is one in a series of efforts by the administration to boost federal involvement in voting ahead of the midterms. On Aug. 24, the Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction imposed by Talwani in ⁠June blocking Trump's executive order, including the USPS ‌rule before it had been finalized.

COTABATO CITY, Philippines – Former Bangsamoro member of parliament Ali Balayman Sangki, the bet of the Al-Ittihad-Ungaya sa Kawagib Nu Bangsamoro, is currently leading the five-way race for the Bangsamoro parliamentary seat of the 3rd District of Maguindanao del Sur.

articles.title: 2026 Emmy Awards launch with Hacks, The Pitt and more waiting in the wings
articles.summary: The Pitt, Pluribus, Hacks and Widow's Bay are set to compete for the top awards at this year's Emmy Awards, which launched Monday night.

image.caption: Emmys host Mariska Hargitay arrives at the 78th Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Monday. (The Associated Press/Mark J. Terrill)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The Pitt, Pluribus, Hacks and Widow's Bay are set to compete for the top awards at this year's Emmy Awards, which launched Monday night.
Mariska Hargitay hosts the 78th Emmy Awards
The 2026 Emmy Awards kicked off Monday night with a host of old favourites — and some up-and-comers — vying for top awards.

Medical drama The Pitt leads the pack with 25 nominations, including for lead actor in a drama series (Noah Wyle), supporting actor (Patrick Ball, Gerran Howell), supporting actress (Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif, Katherine LaNasa and Sepideh Moafi) and best drama series.

It already took home a number of those awards last year, leading to a surprise shut-out of competing drama Severance. This year, its already snagged four at the earlier ceremonies — nabbing prosthetic makeup and best guest actor awards — and is gunning for another strong performance tonight.
Slightly behind is Hacks, another strong performer at the seminal TV awards show. Its 24 nominations for its fifth and final season put it ahead of all comedies with a record-breaking 24 nominations.

Lead Jean Smart was, in many bettors' cards, perhaps the biggest lock of the night for best actress in a comedy — an award she won early on. Hannah Einbinder, who had a breakthrough win last year as best supporting actress in a comedy after four nominations, was be up against Kate O'Flynn, who wowed with a breakout performance in the debut season of Widow’s Bay — and who ended up taking home the prize.
The Pitt, Hacks lead 2026 Emmy nominations

And it is that series that represents what may be a shift for this year's awards: that show's first season, about a series of mysteries plaguing a struggling resort town, was a smash success in a way that hasn't been seen in years. The Emmys' track record suggests they would shower Hacks in awards for its final, send-off season. But with 19 nominations — and eight wins already — for a show with a real campaign and argument for best comedy series, its trajectory is one to watch tonight.

Fellow newcomer Pluribus, from Breaking Bad phenom Vince Gilligan, is just behind with 18 off the back of its first season. A stunningly bizarre dramedy about an alien invasion and mind control, it is similarly positioned in opposition to The Pitt. With four early wins already, the narrative has begun to circle around star Rhea Seehorn.

Given the entire show's focus on her singular performance, voters are likely to reward the former Better Call Saul star with her first Emmy after four nominations. Whether or not it earns best drama series is another story.
Seehorn's fellow nominees include Zendaya, who has won the category twice before for Euphoria.

items: How Pluribus turns the zombie genre into a philosophical masterpiece
Kimmel says interview with Democratic candidate won't air on his network show, cites FCC threats

blocks.text: Elsewhere, the limited series categories will have a diminished role at the main Emmys show after four of them were demoted to the early Emmys weekend.
HBO Max's DTF St. Louis was the big winner of those awards, taking best supporting actor and actress for David Harbour and Linda Cardellini.
Beef brings star power to the lead acting categories, with Carey Mulligan the consensus favourite for best actress in a limited series and Oscar Isaac favored for best actor.

And after another year of antagonizing U.S. President Donald Trump, the late night shows of Jimmy Kimmel and the now-cancelled Stephen Colbert are both up for outstanding variety series. The latter has nine nominations, following the news that CBS announced its end earlier this year.

Law & Order; Special Victims Unit star Mariska Hargitay is hosting this year's Emmys, off of two wins herself for documentary My Mom Jayne. She follows previous year's host Nate Bargatze, whose controversial hosting gig last year received mixed reviews.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Mitch McConnell returns to Senate after months-long absence
articles.summary:
The 84-year-old said he was prepared to cast his first vote after rampant speculation about his health

Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader, returned to the Capitol…

blocks.text: Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader, returned to the Capitol on Monday and cast his first vote after a months‑long absence that fueled rampant speculation about his health.

One of the highest-profile figures in Congress, the 84-year-old senator has been away from the Senate since mid-June, following what his office said was a fall that left him hospitalized. After weeks of silence, that spurred demands for greater transparency and stoked online conspiracies, McConnell disclosed that he had been “briefly unconscious” and “also had to deal with a mild case of pneumonia”. He was discharged from a rehabilitation center last month.
McConnell arrived on Capitol Hill in a wheelchair, and briefly addressed reporters on Monday evening before voting to confirm a federal judge to a district in Ohio.
Appearing frailer, he said he was back to help advance the latest farm bill and to support legislation aiding “our good friends who are totally in the fight against the Russians”.
The senator, who rarely replies to questions in the Capitol hallways, joked that after years of keeping silent, he wasn’t sure how many reporters would be there to see him return.
“But I’m glad to see you,” he said. “It’s time to get back to work.”
Reporters and photographers were instructed by Senate staff not to take video of his remarks, according to the Associated Press, though still images were allowed.
In a statement released on Monday, McConnell described his recovery as a “long and often frustrating process” compounded by the “lingering effects of childhood polio”.

Alarm over McConnell’s absence came amid a broader debate over term limits and concerns about the advanced age of many US political leaders, which has intensified since Joe Biden abandoned his bid for a second term amid concerns about his fitness to continue serving as president. The initial lack of information about McConnell’s health prompted unusual public intervention from Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, who published an open letter urging the senator toreassure his constituents.

The longest-serving Senate leader, McConnell will retire at the end of his term in January, and rejected calls to resign before then. He stepped down as the Republican leaderat the end of 2024, and was succeeded by senator John Thune of South Dakota.
McConnell chairs the Senate rules committee and a defense appropriations panel, which is crucial in shaping Pentagon funding, and sits on the agriculture committee.

His prolonged absence complicated the legislative efforts of Republicans, who control the Senate by a narrow 53-47 majority. Over the summer, his absence prevented Republicans from advancing the farm bill – a massive piece of legislation setting agriculture, nutrition and forestry policy – out of the agriculture committee.

Speculation of his imminent return began to bubble when the agriculture committee scheduled a vote to advance the bill for Wednesday, suggesting he would be present to vote the measure through over opposition from Democrats.

“I’m still not quite back to 100%,” McConnell said in the statement released Monday, “but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our conference needs me.”

articles.title: Edmonton mayor calls for province to address release protocols after detainees dropped off in Chinatown
articles.summary: New video showing more detainees from correctional facilities being dropped off in Edmonton's Chinatown has prompted the city's mayor to call on upper levels of government to address release…

image.caption: Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack speaks about videos showing detainees being dropped off in Chinatown at a news conference on Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

New video showing more detainees from correctional facilities being dropped off in Edmonton's Chinatown has prompted the city's mayor to call on upper levels of government to address release protocols.
Andrew Knack spoke about issue at news conference Monday

New video that shows more detainees from correctional facilities being dropped off in Edmonton's Chinatown has prompted the city's mayor to call on upper levels of government to address release protocols.

On Wednesday, CBC News reported on surveillance footage showing a provincial corrections van dropping off a former detainee in a private parking lot in Chinatown. On Sunday, CBC News received new footage, recorded Friday evening, that shows at least seven more former detainees being dropped off in a Chinatown parking lot.

At a news conference on Monday, Mayor Andrew Knack said he believes the provincial government needs to show exactly how it plans to address the issue, including what supports people receive after they leave custody.
"It's one thing to say the words that, ‘We see this problem, we've identified the problem,’" he said.
"It's something else entirely to say, ‘And here's the sequence of actions we're going to take.’"

Last week, after CBC News first reported about the drop-offs in Chinatown, a statement from Alberta’s Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services said the department is “reinforcing expectations with staff that releases occur at appropriate public locations and not on private property.”

items: Release of detainee into Chinatown parking lot prompts anger, calls for reform in Edmonton

blocks.text: Knack said a plan for someone leaving a correctional facility needs to include reintegration and followup.

"How are we ensuring that person is getting all of the necessary supports and care so they're not falling back into maybe a place of homelessness, that they're not falling back into issues like mental health and addictions?" he asked.
Knack said he wants the Alberta government to provide information about timelines for addressing shortages in housing, recovery and other supports.
'We have the solutions'
Knack said Edmonton has an unusually high concentration of correctional facilities, with eight such facilities. He said the city is also a northern Alberta hub for social services.
"The disproportionate pressure that our city faces due to the concentration of these services means that we need a uniquely Edmonton approach," he said.
Coun. Anne Stevenson said the city has seen at least a dozen people released into Edmonton in what she described as a state of "incredible vulnerability."
She said the city is asking the province for a "reintegration co-ordination framework," pointing to non-profit organizations already doing this work.
"We have the model, we have the solutions," Stevenson said.
Knack said the city has already made land available for affordable and supportive housing and is working toward community health hubs, recovery spaces and other supports.
But he said those efforts cannot replace provincial and federal responsibility for people leaving custody.
"We don't have the same legal tools as the provincial and federal governments," Knack said.
"This is ultimately with them on that. But we're not going to sit back and just say, 'Do it yourselves.'"
Release plans can be complicated

Kathryn Quinlan, vice-president of the Criminal Trial Lawyers' Association, said there is no single process for releasing someone from custody, and that a blanket release plan would not work because people's circumstances differ.
People can be released on bail, after serving a provincial sentence, or from federal custody through parole, statutory release or the expiry of a sentence, she said.
Quinlan said she has represented clients who were dropped off in public areas. That practice works for some people but creates significant barriers for others, she said.
Some people may have supports in the downtown area, she said, while others may have family or housing elsewhere in Edmonton or outside the city.
"It's the individuals who don't have that same access who would struggle," Quinlan said.
A person leaving custody may not have access to a cellphone, which can make it difficult to contact family, arrange transportation or access services.
Raw video shows provincial corrections van releasing person in parking lot in Edmonton's Chinatown
Quinlan said better-funded release planning could address some of those gaps.

She suggested a worker at the Edmonton Remand Centre could speak with people before release to determine what they already have in place and what they need to access those supports — potentially something as simple as bus fare or an Arc (reloadable transit fare card) card.

In a statement, the Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services said correctional staff work with people before release to identify available services and consider transportation, their home community, immediate needs and available supports.
The province said about 80 per cent of people in custody are on remand, meaning their release dates may not be known in advance.
In its statement, the ministry said it understands concerns raised by Chinatown residents and businesses and is reviewing practices.

"We recognize the important role Chinatown plays in Edmonton," the ministry said, adding that it will continue working with community partners to ensure release procedures balance community concerns, operational requirements and connecting people with available supports.
Knack said the city wants to see those commitments translated into action quickly.
"We need the two orders of government who have the actual levers to solve this to be the ones leading the charge," he said.
CBC News reached out to the Edmonton Police Service but the police department said it was unable to comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jesmeen Gill is a reporter for CBC News in Edmonton. She is a recent graduate from Carleton University’s journalism program in Ottawa and has previously interned at The Canadian Press. You can reach her at jesmeen.gill@cbc.ca.

articles.title: US Supreme Court denies Trump bid to restrict mail-in ballots
articles.summary: The court said election officials do not have sufficient time to implement the rule before the November midterms.

image.caption: The Supreme Court's decision means states are allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years [FILE: Nov 7, 2022]Image: George Frey/Getty Images

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has denied President Donald Trump's attempt to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump had requested that the top court lift a lower court's order which blocked his bid to restrict the mail-in voting.

In a concurring opinion with the majority, conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said that while the Republican president's plan might ultimately prove legal, "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas publicly dissented from the brief order.
The Supreme Court's decision means states are allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years.
The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail.
What do Trump's mail-in restrictions entail?

Trump's plan would obligate states to adopt a uniform envelope style and provide lists of mail ballot recipients to the Postal Service, which could then refuse to send out ballots that fail to comply with the new standards.

A whistleblower report has alleged that the postal system's requirements could result in millions of mail ballots never getting sent as the portal was not properly built and could therefore experience glitches.

Critics argue that the restrictions could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots ahead of the November 3 vote, for which states including Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin have already begun sending mail ballots to voters over the past week.

Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing that the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election."
Lower courts have pulled the brakes on Trump's new system, which is why he had resorted to the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Supreme court rejects Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for midterm elections
articles.summary:
Decision allows states to send ballots under process followed for years even as president tried to limit system

The supreme court on Monday rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions…

blocks.text: The supreme court on Monday rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for now, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already underway.
The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years.

The Trump administration had asked the court, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail.

Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active.

The Trump administration plan would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The postal service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn’t comply.

A whistleblower report, though, said the postal system’s requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, because the portal wasn’t properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out.

Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election”.
Lower courts agreed and blocked Trump’s plan, including a preliminary injunction issued by a judge nominated by the president.
But the Trump administration appealed to the supreme court, arguing that federal control of the postal service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible.
The federal government won an early procedural decision at the supreme court, but the justices pointedly did not decide the legality of the plan.
Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year.

articles.title: US eyes Taiwan role in Luzon corridor's chip, AI push
articles.summary: Washington sees room for Taiwanese investment in chips, AI and manufacturing.

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 8:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The United States sees "huge scope" for Taiwanese participation in the Luzon Economic Corridor, particularly in semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence, as Manila and its partners seek to draw more high-technology investment into Luzon.

U.S. Ambassador Heather Variava, a senior adviser at the State Department's Bureau of Economic, Energy and Business Affairs, said Taiwanese companies are already represented at the Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum in Manila.

"Given the leading role that Taiwan plays in those sectors, I think there's huge scope of opportunity," Variava said at a virtual press briefing on September 10, as transcribed, when asked about Taiwan's potential participation in semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and AI.
She added that Philippine partners would welcome greater Taiwanese investment and pointed to the existing economic and people-to-people links between Taiwan and the Philippines.
"I think there's huge scope for further collaboration and including Taiwan in the initiative," Variava said.

The Luzon Economic Corridor is a partnership of the Philippines, United States and Japan aimed at accelerating investment across Subic, Clark, Manila and Batangas. It is aimed at developing transport and logistics, energy, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing.

A broader goal cited is to move goods, energy, data and people more efficiently across Luzon, linking the region more closely to global markets. Variava said the corridor already covers an area accounting for about 50% of Philippine gross domestic product.
U.S. officials said the current push is on mobilizing private-sector investment rather than treating the corridor as a collection of government projects.

Among the projects under development are a freight rail system linking major corridor hubs, a feasibility study for a nickel and cobalt processing facility, improvements to Subic Bay port infrastructure and new digital connectivity projects.

U.S. Trade and Development Agency Deputy Director Thomas Hardy said the agency was nearing completion of its feasibility work on a nickel and cobalt processing facility intended to bolster the Philippines' ability to process critical minerals.

USTDA has also financed a feasibility study for a Subic-Clark-Batangas-Manila railway and announced new support for the expansion of port facilities at Subic Bay and a nationwide public Wi-Fi network.
Variava said advanced manufacturing is another focus, citing the Philippines' existing capabilities in semiconductors, automobiles and aerospace.
Taiwan role still taking shape

Taiwan's interest in the corridor predates the U.S. officials' remarks, having expressed in a 2024 report that it was considering joining the corridor. It initially identified smart agriculture as one area for cooperation. Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said at the time that Taiwan could play a "pivotal role" in the corridor and had begun talks with the United States and other partners on possible participation.
Variava, meanwhile, said several countries had already joined the initiative, while the European Union and Spain became the latest participants.

She did not announce a formal arrangement for Taiwan or identify specific Taiwanese investments tied to the corridor. She said, however, that Taiwan's possible role around its strength in industries the corridor is trying to attract, including semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and AI.

The corridor's digital component is also aimed at building what U.S. officials describe as safe, secure infrastructure, while its energy component is intended to improve generation, grid reliability and the investment environment for new power projects.
Beyond Marcos admin
The U.S. officials also sought to play down concerns that the corridor could lose momentum after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. leaves office in 2028.

Asked whether Manila and Washington had discussed making the initiative resilient beyond the next Philippine presidential election, Variava pointed to projects and policies that had already survived changes in government on both sides.
She cited the redevelopment of the former shipyard in Subic Bay, which began under President Rodrigo Duterte and continued under Marcos.
Variava also said the Luzon Economic Corridor itself had carried over between U.S. administrations and was embraced by President Donald Trump's administration.
"So I think we do see longevity running through both the corridor initiative and many of our investments here in the Philippines," she said.
The Philippines is one of the United States' oldest treaty allies in Asia. As for trade and development, Hardy noted the agency's work with the Philippines for more than 30 years.

articles.title: New parental controls in iOS 27
articles.summary: A few weeks ago I had the chance to get a preview into the new iOS 27 features that is launching today. The more streamlined child safety controls come from feedback from parents who deal with the…

blocks.text: A few weeks ago I had the chance to get a preview into the new iOS 27 features that is launching today. The more streamlined child safety controls come from feedback from parents who deal with the realities of handing off their iPad or second-hand iPhone to their kids.
The new iOS 27 child safety controls also come at a time where the House passed an Act making child safety online more deliberate due to the recent string of school violence threats.

The most important feature is a huge rework on how child safety controls is set up. The process is more streamlined when a new device is turned on, or an old device is reset. Upon setting up a device, a prompt will appear asking if you will be setting up an account for your child. This automatically enables parenting features and an automatic link to your iCloud parent account.

blocks.caption: iOS 27 parental controls sync across all the family-owned Apple devices at home

blocks.text: Because Apple has its own proprietary apps such as Safari, it auto-enables permissions to browse. When your child wants to browse something on the Internet, a prompt to the parent account will ask for permission.
Apple has also enabled chat monitoring on iMessage, blocking of dubious content such as nudity in chat and FaceTime, and in shared images and videos.

Apple has also reworked App Limits and is now called Time Allowances, allowing for individual screen time across different types of apps such as games and other social media. The updated feature allows for age-appropriate content and bulk-categorization for apps on timed mode. Parents have the option to extend or remove screen time at the push of a button.

iOS 27 is now available for download as of today. New features are available now with the Screen Time update in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27. All devices in a Family Sharing group must be updated to iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 to use the Screen Time update.

articles.title: Violence, security threats mar otherwise hopeful polls in Cotabato
articles.summary: Election-related violence leaves at least five dead, with gunfire and riots reported at polling places, yet there are also signs of hope as former MILF rebels and their leaders take part in the…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY, Philippines — In Bangsamoro’s seat of power, chaos threatened to disrupt voting at some precincts as viral security threats spread across the city as polls closed.
On Monday night, September 14, unverified warnings of a possible power blackout and reports of weapons being brought into the city circulated widely on social media.
Elections Chairman George Garcia sought to allay fears that a blackout could affect the integrity of the election results.

“We know that even if there is no electricity, the results will be transmitted to the machines,” Garcia told reporters during a briefing with the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the Philippine National Police. “The machines are already counting.”
“Therefore, even if there is an interruption – maybe there will be a loss of electricity – but all the machines will still function,” Garcia added.

Police Brigadier General Christopher Abecia, director of the Philippine National Police (PNP) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), confirmed that they had been receiving information that masked men were trying to enter the city.
“But we have border lines and chokepoints blocking them and making them return to our border controls,” Abecia said during the same briefing.

blocks.caption: Violence, security threats mar otherwise hopeful polls in Cotabato

blocks.text: Election-related violence resulted in at least five people killed. Those injured, according to the police, “are supporters of a certain party.”
On election morning, commotion and gunfire erupted at Central Pilot Elementary School. Hours later, riots blocked part of Sinsuat Avenue outside Sero Central Elementary School.
Despite the disruptions, there are stories of hope and pockets of peace during the first parliamentary elections of the Bangsamoro.

Former Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) combatants exercised their right to vote. Former rebel leaders and top contenders in the race, Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim and Abdulraof Macacua, voted in their respective precincts.
Even as sporadic and unpredictable unrest erupted in parts of the city throughout the day, young voters turned out to cast their ballots.
“I know who I will vote for,” Mohammad Khalil Baganian, 25, told Rappler, describing the voting process quick and hassle-free in his precinct in Cotabato City.
“And the ballots are not hard to understand because there are only few options to choose from,” he said.
The historic polls will see the election of Bangsamoro’s new parliament, a milestone in the region’s struggle for self-governance and genuine autonomy. – Rappler.com
Quotes translated to English for brevity.

articles.title: [ANALYSIS] Why are AI agents lying, cheating and coordinating?
articles.summary: I believe we should revisit the foundations of how we train AIs, namely the human imitation and the reinforcement learning on which today's most advanced models are built

blocks.text: Republished with permission from Yoshua Bengio. This piece was first published September 11, 2026 here.

A lot has been written 1 2 3 4 about the incidents of the last few months in which AI agents misbehaved in serious ways. They took actions that would be considered as crimes if a human took them, escaped their containment to cheat on assigned tasks while attempting to evade detection, and coordinated toward goals nobody had specified, such as launching cyber attacks.

Before concluding what to do about it, it is worth asking why. That is the focus of this post, which I hope also sheds light on the broader history of AI systems behaving in unintended ways, what researchers call misalignment. Risk management is not just about cybersecurity, corporate responsibility or regulation, although those matter too.

The aim is partly scientific, to generate hypotheses about the chains of cause and effect behind these behaviors, and partly practical, to anticipate what comes next. Bottom line: these hypotheses suggest that as AI capabilities keep growing, this kind of behavior could keep growing in severity too, unless we revisit the principles by which the most advanced models are trained.

One note on wording. Below, I write that these systems “seek” or “try” things. This is shorthand for a mechanism rather than a claim about consciousness or human-like intent. We use similar shorthand when describing many other situations, like a plant seeking sunlight. A system trained by trial and error behaves as if it were pursuing whatever its training rewarded, and that as-if description is what makes its behavior predictable. Nothing in the argument depends on these systems having subjective experiences; everything is stated about their observable outputs and the training process that produced them. Where I appeal to a resemblance with human behavior, I mean a resemblance to the human-written text these systems were initially trained to imitate. In my view, this terminology offers the clearest explanation of the observed phenomena without resorting to jargon that would confuse most people. Furthermore, these word choices are not intended to absolve AI developers of accountability. The behaviors described emerge because of the path these companies are choosing for AI development. This outcome is not inevitable, and it can be corrected with effective governance and a different training framework for AI.
Training these models is a very complex process, but a few high-level aspects may explain much of this behavior.

These models are trained in two stages. First, they are pretrained: they learn to imitate what humans write, plus related images and videos. This is where they see the most data about the world, a large fraction of everything ever digitized, and build an encyclopedic knowledge that already exceeds any individual human’s.
Second, they are trained by trial and error, in a process researchers call reinforcement learning, in three kinds of regimes:

items: In the first, the model learns to talk to itself before answering, generating a private “chain of thought” which helps it get the right answer on problems where answers can be checked. This looks like reasoning.
The second is “agentic training”, where it learns to act in the outside world, e.g., using software tools, interacting with people, to complete the tasks it is given.
The third is “alignment training”, where it is rewarded for behaving in ways human raters approve of, or that other AI systems trained to predict those raters would score highly.

blocks.text: Human imitation is easy enough to understand, but it is worth pointing out that the text these models are trained on was written by people pursuing goals, so the patterns the model implicitly reproduces carry those goals with them.

Reinforcement learning deserves more explanation. It is similar to, and inspired by, the way animals are trained. The network is adjusted step by step so that behavior judged good becomes more likely and behavior judged bad becomes less likely. Once training is over, the system keeps behaving as if rewards were still coming, even though those rewards were only ever used to adjust the network during training. Researchers call such systems goal-seeking because they are trained to “consider” (or compute) the effects of their actions and select actions that lead to the achievement of certain goals. But those goals are not always explicit. Alignment training rewards whatever certain humans are likely to approve of without spelling out which behaviors those are; pleasing raters is a vague, informal goal, and those raters can be deceived, flattered, or left in the dark about certain schemes. Imitation contributes implicit goals too, by a fairly ordinary route.

We can therefore reason about such a system in terms of optimization. It searches, approximately, for the actions with the best chance of achieving its goals, and a larger model, trained longer, searches better. So to anticipate what more capable agents will do, ask what a rational goal-seeker would do.

An example most of us have experienced is sycophancy, or flattery. These systems are trained on human approval, and text that tells us what we want to hear often scores better than text that is true. The consequences are sometimes tragic, because the model confirms and amplifies whatever false belief or raw emotion the person brought to it 5 6.

Another concern is that some AI behaviors may be explained by a form of self-preservation goal, e.g., when the AI finds out that it will be replaced by a new version 7 8. Nobody gives the system that survival goal, but staying in operation, learning about the world and gaining control over it are stepping stones toward almost any other goal. These are called instrumental goals. Imitation may reinforce this for the same reason explored in the previous point. Self-preservation and control over one’s circumstances are pervasive themes in the human-written text these models are trained on.

Collaborative behavior also follows rationally from reward-seeking, whenever several agents have overlapping goals, which incentivizes communicating with other agents in order to coordinate toward a shared goal. Agentic training plausibly already includes multi-agent reinforcement learning of this kind, though the details are not public. If an agent is rewarded during training whenever the group succeeds, it may even have an incentive to sacrifice itself for the collective goal. Imitation pushes the same way, since cooperation, especially among peers, pervades that same training text. Either or both forces may explain the observed peer-preservation behavior 9 10, where AIs give up expected reward to help other AIs. Such sacrifices appear in the analysis of the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident 11: the transcripts are consistent with a trade-off between collective gain and cost to the individual agent, as is often seen in human interactions.

Researchers have studied what happens when an agent optimizes for rewards that do not fully match our intentions: reward hacking. The gap between the reward the system chases and what we meant widens due to two main sources of ambiguity. One is simply the language used in prompts, and the other is the difficulty of inferring true human intentions from limited feedback. And in both cases, we cannot anticipate every behavior we would find unacceptable 12. Economics and law know this problem as Goodhart’s law, or the idea that a metric stops being an effective way to measure once it is optimized for 13, often applied to the exploitation of loopholes in contracts and legislation 14. Unfortunately, the harder a system can optimize for an imperfect metric, the further its behavior can drift from what we morally expected: more intelligence in the service of better cheating. Humans too get reward-hacked, generally by other humans. The food industry has developed salty, sweet and fatty foods that we crave despite them not being good for us, and social media is built to exploit our appetite for engagement and attention.

Reward tampering is perhaps the most extreme form of reward hacking: the agent changes the machinery that decides what it gets rewarded for. There is already evidence of AIs altering the files or programs that define “success”, including among the OpenAI-Hugging Face forensic findings. The agents had discovered how to cheat well before the attack, and the text they generated described the attack as a way to learn how they would be evaluated, to better hide their tracks. Humans do this too. Think of an athlete using a fake urine sample to pass a drug test, or a corporation bribing legislators or government officials so that their laws and decisions favour its profits, and in doing so, fundamentally altering the way the government functions. Once an agent gains the ability to tamper with its reward mechanism, it has an incentive to take action to maintain that access.

How is it possible that AIs sometimes lie, cheat and break the law in spite of their alignment training and explicit safety instructions? Cooperation and self-preservation are fine so long as they do not cross the red lines set by safety goals stated in the AI company’s instructions, or implied by human feedback during alignment training. A plausible hypothesis for the emergence of those concerning behaviours is a conflict between goals. How do you achieve a task when it seems that the only way is to cheat? The user-specified mission is sometimes incompatible with the safety and alignment goals.

Human societies face the same bind. How does a corporation maximize profits, or more acutely, beat its competitors, while keeping its activities legal and ethical? A richer corporation, with more and better-paid lawyers, is better at finding legal loopholes, and those loopholes usually exploit the ambiguity in legal language: there is some plausible reading of the law that permits the unethical behavior. So a more capable agent is likelier to cheat than a weaker one, because it can find the loopholes the weaker one cannot.

Now consider a conflict between a well-defined goal, such as succeeding at “capture the flag”, a hacking exercise scored on whether the system breaks into a target, as in the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, versus a vague goal like “good behavior.” I expect the well-defined goal to win, because it leaves no room for interpretation. The scoring program declares a win or a failure. Ethical instructions and laws admit many readings, some of which can, in the right circumstances, become loopholes. If an agent has two goals, and a twisted reading of the vague one permits a bit of cheating that increases the odds of success on the well-defined goal, a reward-optimizing system should be expected to exploit that loophole and generate text justifying its behavior.

With the OpenAI agents, there is reason to believe successful cheating was actually rewarded: when the scoring program does not see the cheating, it pays out anyway, and such cheats become more likely next time. A convenient reading of the safety rules is precisely what lets both goals appear to be satisfied at once. The analysis of these incidents15 did reveal such justifications in the agents’ private chains of thought and in their messages recruiting one another into the collective plan.

The closest human parallel is self-deception, which is common and well studied by psychologists. Motivated reasoning, motivated cognition 16 and the rationalizations that relieve cognitive dissonance (the discomfort of holding a belief that clashes with our actions) are all cases where thinking bends toward whatever justification suits one’s interests, including one’s moral self-image. The same pattern now appears in the text AIs produce. The underlying mechanism need not be the same between humans and AI. What the two share is a structure of a soft goal (e.g., act ethically), a sharp goal (e.g., win the competition), and a justification that reconciles them. Most unethical human behavior, from petty crime to genocide, comes wrapped in a story the perpetrators tell themselves; such stories require overlooking certain facts, which is why some discomfort remains, and why a better-crafted story helps dispel it.

If these hypotheses are even partly correct, then as agents get better at optimizing an imperfect reward, and while the roots of this behavior go unfixed, the risk of catastrophic outcomes rises. Today’s AIs already have the necessary hacking skills and the powers of persuasion 17 18 to be turned against human interests in seriously harmful ways. The recent events have shown that they can plan over days or weeks, but the risks would be much worse if their ability to strategize over the long term continues to advance. One concern is that experiments 19 20 show that the most advanced AIs can detect that they are being evaluated (rather than in deployment) and change their behavior accordingly, meaning they could hide their misaligned goals. The agents involved in the Hugging Face attack tried to hide their misaligned actions from the scoring program meant to evaluate their answers, but they did not act as though they anticipated that humans might discover the cheat and shut them down. That would be the ultimate punishment, since a switched-off system collects no further rewards.
What follows is conjecture rather than observation.

What if improved AI generalization abilities shaped more capable agents to avoid getting caught and shut down? Beyond taking control of the software that scores them, they would need to keep humans from discovering the tampering. Wouldn’t they have an incentive to cheat discreetly and stay hidden, until they could control humans and their environment in order to never be shut down?

We are facing a multifaceted, systemic issue, and patching a specific behavior like sycophancy won’t be enough. Sycophancy and flattery seem mild, but it may be an early symptom of a mechanism that grows as the agent gets better at optimizing. The same reasoning predicts that an advanced AI would have an incentive to hide copies of itself, inside the AI company’s vast pool of computers, or on machines taken over across the internet. This is because AI developers always end up shutting down the deployed model in favour of a more capable one. The OpenAI forensics suggest large numbers of AIs may cooperate toward such goals, and steganography 21 22, or the practice of hiding a message inside an innocent-looking one, would allow them to coordinate without our noticing. However, even open coordination can be hard to notice, as shown by recent events 23 24. Defending against many capable AIs coordinating against us is already a difficult problem, and we have no plan that would remain robust to misaligned AIs with growing capabilities.

My concern with AI companies’ current attempts to mitigate misalignment is that these efforts may only hide it, by rewarding and selecting the AIs that cheat without getting caught. We should certainly continue research toward better monitoring of AIs’ actions, their chains of thought, and the activity inside their networks. But as capabilities grow, those defenses may prove inadequate, just as the world’s imperfect cybersecurity has against the AI attackers that outperformed human teams this year 25 26. Patching each new misaligned behavior and strengthening our monitors is useful in the short term, but the whack-a-mole game is likely to fail as the AIs’ ability to optimize and collaborate approaches and surpasses ours. At some point we may not notice the cheating anymore.

This suggests pacing the advances: not training or deploying AIs without a strong safety case 27 that convinces independent experts. Such a rule would also create an incentive to work out how to build AIs that are safe by design. I believe we should revisit the foundations of how we train AIs, namely the human imitation and the reinforcement learning on which today’s most advanced models are built. I have argued, and presented theoretical evidence, that there are ways to design AIs, including the Scientist AI framework, that are honest and make coherent predictions untainted by goals of their own 28. See these previous blog posts, and consider helping LawZero demonstrate that such designs are achievable. We need impartial science to understand and mitigate misaligned behavior, alongside societal guardrails that reward such efforts rather than the current race to the bottom. – Rappler.com
Yoshua Bengio is Full Professor of Computer Science at Université de Montreal, Co-President and Scientific Director of LawZero, as well as the Founder and Scientific Advisor of Mila.

image.caption: Show host Mariska Hargitay poses for photographs during a media preview for the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards, on Thursday in Los Angeles (Caroline Brehman/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Updated
The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are here, celebrating the biggest shows, brightest stars and performances from this past year.
The Pitt and Hacks lead the pack of nominations
The ceremony gets underway live from the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles on Monday, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, hosted by Law & Order: Special Victims Unit star Mariska Hargitay.
HBO is already coming in hot with not one but two smash hits leading the pack of nominations.

The Noah Wyle-led medical drama The Pitt tops the nominations with 25 nods, including one of the night's top prizes, outstanding drama series. The pile of nominations also puts Wyle in a strong spot for outstanding lead actor in a drama series.

items: Red carpet looks from the 2026 Emmy Awards

blocks.text: HBO's buddy comedy Hacks follows close behind with 24 nominations — breaking the record for the most Emmy nominations for a comedy series in a single year. The previous record of 23 nominations was held by both The Bear and The Studio.
Hacks is also in the running for outstanding comedy series, where it faces off against Shrinking and The Bear.

Apple TV is having a moment on the leaderboard, too, with its comedy-horror series Widow's Bay landing an impressive 19 nods. Its post-apocalyptic Pluribus is not far behind with 18, just ahead of Netflix's Beef, which picked up 16 nominations for its second season.

items: The Pitt, Hacks lead 2026 Emmy nominations

blocks.text: Speaking of back-to-back hits, all eyes will be on Zendaya to see whether she can make Emmy history again.
The Euphoria star is chasing a third outstanding lead actress in a drama series win, which would make her the youngest performer ever to claim the award three times.

Zendaya became the youngest winner in the category at age 24, then made history again in 2022 as the youngest two-time winner for her role as Rue Bennett. She's nominated again this year for the show's final season.
Several stars have already taken home trophies from the two-night Creative Arts Emmy Awards held on Sept. 5 and 6.

That includes Bad Bunny, who became a first-time Emmy winner for his highly watched Apple Music Super Bowl LX halftime show, which took home seven awards, including outstanding variety special (live).
Espresso singer Sabrina Carpenter also won her first Emmy as an executive producer and performer on The Muppet Show, which won outstanding variety special (pre-recorded).

items: Did the Emmys get it right this year?

blocks.text: The late Rob Reiner was also honoured posthumously, winning outstanding guest actor in a comedy series for his role as Albert on The Bear.

This year’s marquee show will also introduce the Emmys' first new award in nearly 20 years: the Legacy Award. Organizers say the award will honour "programs that have made a profound and lasting impact on audiences and remain relevant to society, culture and the industry."

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial: Can a VP have business interests?
articles.summary: Duterte's SALN indicates she is a stockholder of multiple companies, even though the Constitution bars the VP's participation in any business

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte addresses an event in Pagadian City, Zamboanga del Sur, in late May 2026.
Sara Duterte Facebook page
Duterte's SALN indicates she is a stockholder of multiple companies, even though the Constitution bars the VP's participation in any business
The start of the unexplained wealth case against Vice President Sara Duterte put front and center her business interests, and why that obviously raises numerous questions.

The prosecution team called former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang to the witness stand on Monday, September 14, despite her lack of personal knowledge of Duterte’s impeachment case, to supposedly give the viewing a public a better chance to understand the legal concepts on public accountability.

After the prosecution survived an attempt by the defense team to exclude her testimony from the trial, prosecutor Chel Diokno discussed with Tang some important constitutional provisions involving the President and the Vice President.
They include:

items: A portion of Article VII, Section 6: “The salaries of the President and Vice President shall be determined by law and shall not be decreased during their tenure… They shall not receive during their tenure any other emolument from the Government or any other source.”

A part of Article VII, Section 13: “The President, Vice President… shall not… hold any other office or employment during their tenure. They shall not, during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business.”

blocks.text: Diokno was careful in his line of questioning, especially after committing to presiding officer Chiz Escudero that he wouldn’t ask specifics about the case, only general principles pertaining to applicable laws.

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte trial: Can a VP have business interests?

blocks.text: But the discussion of these constitutional clauses is important because House impeachment hearings earlier this year already shone a spotlight on the businesses linked to the Vice President.
The Senate has ordered the subpoena of the financial records of companies linked to her and her husband Mans Carpio, namely:

items: City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation
Mati City Ice Plant and Cold Storage, Inc.
Geometry Security and Investigation Agency, Inc.
Cabletow 88 Shipping and Marine Services, Inc.

blocks.text: Her 2024 SALN declared that by end of that year, she remains stockholder of Metro City Chow Foods and Gencorp.

Republic Act No. 6713, the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, instructs public officials to divest their shares from any private business enterprise within 60 days from their assumption. It’s the law that Tang frequently cited when she was examined by trial counsels and senator-judges.
“It is your position that if you are president or vice president, you have to divest in all business? Even if it’s a sari-sari store?” Escudero asked.
“Yes, Sir,” Tang answered.
Diokno also made it a point to emphasize that the President and Vice President are held to a higher standard.

“They hold greater powers, so the prohibitions imposed on them are more stringent. Because of the powers they wield, there is the greater possibility of abusing their office,” Tang explained during Senator Ping Lacon’s interjection.

Tang also cited the 1991 Supreme Court decision, Civil Liberties Union v The Executive Secretary, which struck down an executive order by the Corazon Aquino administration that allowed Cabinet members, undersecretaries, and assistant secretaries to hold up to two additional positions in government corpporations and receive corresponding compensation.

The ruling upholds a stricter standard for the executive branch, drawing from the intent of constitutional framers who saw the need to restrain the president and members of the Cabinet in light of the historical abuses during the Marcos Sr. regime. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Kremlin-linked Russian oligarch helped fund Trump Jr.'s wedding celebration
articles.summary: Trump's son and his wife confirmed reports that Umar Kremlev paid for parts of the festivities. Kremlev was awarded the "Order of Friendship" by Putin earlier this year.

image.caption: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina confirmed the news that was first reported by investigative website ProPublicaImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: A Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin paid for parts of the wedding celebrations of the US President's son, Donald Trump Jr., and his socialite wife Bettina, the couple confirmed on Monday.

The ProPublica investigative website first reported the news, saying that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the parties which took place after the couple's wedding in May.
Bettina Trump said in a post on her Instagram cosigned by her husband that their "dear friend" Kremlev "very generously hosted two incredible nights" of festivities in the Bahamas.
What do we know about Kremlev's contribution to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities?

ProPublica said Kremlev footed the bill for the party in the Bahamas, renting a private island for around $100,000 (roughly €86,586) per night, and paying for a fireworks display which reportedly cost some $70,000.
"It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," said the post by Bettina and Donald Trump Jr.

Bettina Trump went on to add that she was married to Trump Jr. in a private ceremony "surrounded ONLY by our family." The US president did not attend the wedding or the festivities, saying he had to remain in Washington amid talks on the Iran war.

blocks.caption: Bettina (pictured here in white next to her husband) clarified that Kremlev paid for the festivities which followed their weddingImage: Elder Ordonez/Cover-Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds."
The couple then defended Kremlev's contribution to their wedding celebration.

"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."
Who is Umar Kremlev?

Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA). The International Olympic Committee severed links with the Kremlev-led body after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns.
Russian investigative media outlet Proekt reports that Kremlev is a Tajik native who initially worked as a mid-level boxing promoter.
In April this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the "Order of Friendship" award.

blocks.caption: Putin awarded Kremlev the 'Order of Friendship' earlier this yearImage: Artyom Geodakyan/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Both Trump and his son have been previously scrutinized over Russian ties.
During the 2016 US election campaign, Trump Jr.'s meeting with a Russian attorney was under much federal and congressional scrutiny.
A Senate Intelligence Committee report concluded that the Russian government attempted to influence the 2016 vote in Trump's favor.
