articles.title: Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows
articles.summary:
Trump administration undermining rule of law at home and worldwide, according to intergovernmental report

Key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50…

blocks.text: Key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, with the global rule of law significantly undermined by the Trump administration’s “threats and actions”, data from a leading thinktank shows.

Around the world, judicial independence, credible elections and freedom of expression, press freedom and access to justice are all at their lowest levels for at least 30 years, according to the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International Idea).
The intergovernmental organisation’s annual Global State of Democracy report is considered the most comprehensive of its kind, covering 174 countries and measuring democratic performance since 1975.

International Idea said the decline in the US was particularly marked, but part of a global trend, with 2025 the 11th consecutive year in which more countries declined than improved democratically – the longest continuous downturn since the thinktank’s records began.

“In 2025, the global challenges to democracy and the difficulty in stemming its erosion were both exemplified and compounded by political developments in the United States,” the report’s authors said.

“President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing longstanding alliances and multilateral cooperation.”

blocks.caption: Donald Trump has made repeated false claims about the integrity of US elections. Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty Images

blocks.text: Kevin Casas-Zamora, International Idea’s secretary general, warned that the risk of conflict rose as democracies deteriorated.

“The key message from our research is that investing in democracy should be at the heart of any country’s security strategy,” he said. “The connection between the erosion of the quality of democracy and increasing conflict is not being made either in policymaking or in the public debate.”

The separate Uppsala Conflict Data Program, based at Uppsala University in Sweden, shows that 2025 had the most violent conflicts – including the most interstate conflicts – of any year in its dataset, which goes back to 1946.

The International Idea report did highlight some positive developments, including in Australia – where civil society groups were consulted on an anti-racism strategy and children’s online privacy among other issues – and in Syria, where the repressive dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad was overthrown.

In Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka, youth-led popular protests unseated long-serving leaders, but, the report noted, “it has proven difficult to create far-reaching, meaningful reform in a short period of time”.

Casas-Zamora said it was clear that events in the US influenced other countries. International Idea added the US to its list of “backsliding” democracies for the first time in 2021, pointing to a “visible deterioration” it said began in 2019.

blocks.caption: Young voters celebrate in Nepal after the election of a new government in March. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: The thinktank bases its assessments on 50 years of democratic indicators, assigning countries to one of three categories: democracies, “hybrid” governments and authoritarian regimes.

Globally, it found rule of law was the weakest area of democracy in 2025, with 71 countries – 41% of those assessed – ranked as low-performing. It was also found to be deteriorating quickly, with 29 countries registering downturns.
“Whatever happens in the US goes global. There is now an epidemic of election denialism, of which the patient zero is the current occupant of the White House,” Casas-Zamor said.

“I am not willing to say the deterioration of the quality of democracy is inevitable or permanent. It can be reversed,” he added. “We live in a volatile world and that means things can happen which create very positive political openings.”
Yet, despite the positive signs in Nepal, Bangladesh and elsewhere, the report paints a bleak picture overall.

“While people continue to push back against democratic deterioration, civic space is narrowing,” its authors wrote. “Civil society and civic engagement have suffered, due in part to the widespread use of strategic lawsuits against public participation, foreign agent laws, and the criminalisation of peaceful protests.”

articles.title: Comelec issues amended rules for BARMM parliament proclamation
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) early Tuesday, Sept. 15, issued an amended guideline for the day of the proclamation of winners in the historic Bangsamoro Autonomous…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) early Tuesday, Sept. 15, issued an amended guideline for the day of the proclamation of winners in the historic Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections.

The poll body directed all winning candidates to bring only four companions during the formal declaration at the 6th Infantry Division, Camp Siongco in Barangay Awang, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte.

These include the regional parliamentary political parties and candidates of the parliamentary district representatives in Maguindanao del Norte, excluding Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur, and special geographic areas.
They are also required to submit the list of complete names of their companions, plate numbers of the vehicles to be used, and the name of each vehicle driver.
The Comelec also warned the candidates against bringing firearms inside the premises.
“Should any firearm/s be brought to the venue, it shall be deposited in accordance with the applicable security protocols,” it said in the issued advisory.
After four postponements, the historic BARMM parliament election was officially conducted in at least 5,212 clustered precincts in 1,186 voting centers across the region early Monday. /jpv

articles.title: Duke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UK
articles.summary:
Committee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residents

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded…

blocks.text: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded security following their return to the UK.
The royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec), which oversees tax-funded security for royalty and public figures, is to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s level of police protection.
The committee met last week to discuss the couple’s case, now they and their children are full-time residents in the UK and not just visitors.
It will be the first risk assessment for Meghan since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.
Harry was granted a review of his security in July but has yet to receive a decision.
The Telegraph has reported that Ravec’s chair informed Harry last week the committee had commissioned a new risk assessment and a separate one for Meghan, in light of their return to the UK.
The committee has reportedly asked the couple to provide their schedules and daily routine, including the school run, to inform their decision.
Last year, Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office after the automatic tax-funded security for him and his family was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.

“The UK is my home,” said Harry in his witness statement. “The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”
The couple returned to the UK on 26 August. Soon after, a formal letter was issued on behalf of King Charles, reiterating their status as non-working royals.

The letter stated the couple were “akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests” and “any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities”.
The Sussexes also decided on Monday to switch their children to a new school just two days after they started, reportedly due to security concerns over the long journey and heavy traffic.

“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a family spokesperson told Hello! magazine.
“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.
“This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”

articles.title: Romualdez moved to Payatas jail, arraignment set Sept. 16
articles.summary: Former speaker was transferred to the Quezon City jail after independent medical review.

blocks.text: September 15, 2026 | 6:50am
Then-speaker of the House Martin Romualdez speaks at the launch of Congress TV 11 in January 2024.
House of Reps / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Former House speaker Martin Romualdez was transferred to the New Quezon City Jail late Monday after government doctors found no medical need for continued hospital confinement, two days before his scheduled arraignment on a P7.44-billion plunder case.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division set Romualdez's arraignment and pre-trial for 8:30 a.m. Wednesday, September 16, according to a resolution released Monday.
During arraignment, Romualdez will be asked to enter a plea to the plunder charge against him.

The anti-graft court also ordered his immediate transfer to the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory after doctors from the Philippine General Hospital testified that he was clinically stable and no longer required inpatient care at an acute care hospital.
Romualdez was transferred from PGH to the jail in Payatas, Quezon City at 10:09 p.m. Monday.
PGH Director Dr. Gerardo Legaspi told the court that Romualdez was "clinically stable" and unlikely to suffer an emergency medical condition if discharged from hospital confinement.
The PGH team said unstable angina was "not demonstrated" during its evaluation and found no acute cerebrovascular event, despite earlier diagnoses cited by Cardinal Santos Medical Center.
Doctors confirmed that Romualdez has chronic coronary artery disease and chronic cerebrovascular disease, but said neither condition currently requires inpatient management.
They also told the court that his response to a stress test was normal and estimated that his annual risk of suffering a heart attack over the next decade was about 3%.
Dr. Henry Fabro, chief medical officer of the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory, assured the court that the facility could manage Romualdez's medical needs.

Fabro said Romualdez could regularly use his CPAP machine, receive prescribed medication and consult his private doctors inside the jail. He could also be transferred to a nearby hospital in an emergency.
Romualdez had sought continued confinement at Cardinal Santos Medical Center after his September 7 arrest.
The Sandiganbayan instead ordered him transferred to PGH on September 11 for an independent medical examination.

Romualdez faces plunder allegations over P7.44 billion in alleged kickbacks from contractors and other parties with interests in flood-control, infrastructure and other government projects. — with reports from The STAR / Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Republican Mitch McConnell returns to U.S. Senate after 3-month absence
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the U.S. Senate on Monday for the first time since June 14, when he was hospitalized after a fall in his home.

image.caption: U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell waves at reporters outside the Senate Chamber after he returned to Capitol Hill on Monday. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the U.S. Senate on Monday for the first time since June 14, when he was hospitalized after a fall in his home.
McConnell has been conspicuously absent since he suffered a fall June 11

McConnell's three-month absence from the Senate generated a flood of criticism and online speculation, as the Kentucky senator initially remained quiet for weeks about his condition. The 84-year-old senator eventually disclosed that he had been "briefly unconscious" due to the fall and had also been treated for mild pneumonia in the hospital.

"My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier," McConnell said in a statement Monday. "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader [John] Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me."

The concerns over McConnell's absence highlighted increasing public concern about the age of lawmakers and their capacity to carry out their duties. Speculation about his condition grew so intense at one point that Kentucky's Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear took the extraordinary step of issuing a public letter asking McConnell to update the public in a "transparent manner."
Mitch McConnell confirms he's alive; his absence, death of other senator complicate Republican power

McConnell's absence was also felt over the summer as Republicans were unable to advance a farm bill out of committee. His return could give Republican leaders a needed vote as they try to advance legislation on cryptocurrency regulation and college sports.

items: Late-night TV hosts skewer Mitch McConnell's proof-of-life photo
U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell breaks silence, says he was hospitalized after a fall

blocks.text: McConnell, who holds the distinction of being the longest-serving Senate leader, is in his final months of his four decades in office. He is retiring at the end of January after one of the most consequential careers in modern politics.
Republicans have nominated U.S. Rep. Andy Barr to replace him, while Democrats have nominated former state lawmaker Charles Booker. McConnell said he is determined to finish out his term.
History of health problems
McConnell had polio in his early childhood and has long acknowledged difficulty as an adult in walking and climbing stairs.

The physician's office in Congress in the July statement said McConnell has "experienced several falls through the year" due to his "post-polio condition." The office said his physical therapy was aimed at reducing the risk of him falling again.
"A comprehensive evaluation by a multidisciplinary team determined that he had no fractures, cardiac abnormalities, stroke, tumor, or hemorrhage," the physician's office said.

items: The U.S. Senate is in turmoil. What does it mean for upcoming midterm elections?

blocks.text: McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1984 and was the Republican leader from 2007 until last year , serving as both majority and minority leader during that period. He has remained active as a rank-and-file senator, showing up for work when the chamber is in session, often using a wheelchair to get around.
But the senator's physical condition has visibly declined in recent years.
He was hospitalized with a concussion in March 2023 and missed several weeks of work after falling in a Washington hotel.

He twice froze up during news conferences after he returned, staring vacantly ahead before colleagues and staff. A year later, he fell and sprained his wrist while walking out of a Republican luncheon.

articles.title: Iconic winter X Games comes to Calgary
articles.summary: The X Games sports competition is coming to Calgary in February next year. WinSport's Canada Olympic Park will host the three-day event beginning Feb. 19.

image.caption: A file photo of WinSport's Canada Olympic Park. The X Games will take over the Calgary venue in February 2027. (Dave Gilson/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
The X Games sports competition is coming to Calgary in February next year. WinSport's Canada Olympic Park will host the three-day event beginning Feb. 19.
WinSport will host 3-day competition in February 2027
The iconic X Games action sports competition is coming to Calgary in February next year.
WinSport's Canada Olympic Park will host the three-day competition beginning Feb. 19, and the city will also see international musical acts Levity and Steve Aoki perform as part of the event.
The Calgary stop marks the first time in the 31-year history of the X Games that the competition will be hosted in Canada.

“X Games is one of those events you dream of hosting in your city,” said Tourism Calgary president and CEO Alisha Reynolds. “There is truly no better city than Calgary to host this electrifying event.”
The event will see some of the world's top skiers and snowboarders compete in events like Big Air, Knuckle Huck, Slopestyle and Superpipe.
Officials estimate roughly 15,000 to 20,000 spectators will attend the three days of competition.
Reynolds estimates the event will bring in roughly $25 million for the city’s visitor economy.
Canadian athletes excited to host

Calgarian Brendan Mackay, a freestyle skier with Team Canada, is excited to have the event come to his hometown. Mackay remembers what a podium finish at his first X Games in 2020 meant for his career.
“That was honestly for me a huge career-defining moment,” said Mackay. “That really set into motion what has been a really great athletic career since then.”
Growing up watching the games on TV inspired Mackay, and he says hosting could have an even bigger impact on the next generation.

blocks.text: Historically Aspen, Colo., has hosted many of the winter X Games events and therefore produced some of the sports' best athletes, says Mackay.
“So I think having that come to Calgary will be so impactful on all the young kids who get to go out and watch it,” he said.
Mike Atkinson breaks down Brendan Mackay's bronze-medal run in men's freeski halfpipe
Professional snowboarder Craig McMorris, who grew up in Saskatchewan and credits monthly trips to Canada Olympic Park for his success, is also excited for the event to finally come to Canada.
“Canada has exported the best action sports talent in the entire world — full stop,” McMorris said. "It’s finally now our time to host the X Games.”
New format for Calgary X Games
In 2026, the X Games launched a new league format where athletes compete individually but also earn points for club teams, adding a championship race that fans can follow throughout the season.
At the X Games Calgary media event on Monday, CEO Jeremy Bloom also unveiled the four clubs for the winter league, which will draft athletes later this week. They include X Games Club Whistler.
“So Canadians will have a club to root for,” Bloom said.

articles.title: Bell plans expansion of Sask. AI data centre, making it largest private investment in province's history
articles.summary: At an investment summit in Toronto hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney, Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic announced the controversial data centre near Regina will be expanded from the original…

image.caption: Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic announces plans to expand the AI data centre located just outside Regina at an investment summit in Toronto on Monday. (CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatoon·New

At an investment summit in Toronto hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney, Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic announced the controversial data centre near Regina will be expanded from the original 300-megawatt facility to one that would eventually need 1.2 gigawatts of power.
Bell Canada announced quadrupling of project near Regina at investment summit in Toronto
Bell Canada announced plans Monday to quadruple the size of a planned AI data centre near Regina, a move that would make it the largest private capital investment in Saskatchewan history.

At an investment summit in Toronto hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney, Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic announced the controversial data centre will be expanded from the original 300-megawatt facility to one that would eventually need 1.2 gigawatts of power.
To achieve the expansion, the telecommunications giant would increase its investment in the so-called Bell AI Fabric to $52 billion.
With Premier Scott Moe standing next to him, Bibic offered praise to the Saskatchewan Party government for creating the investment environment in the province.

"I was asked three specific times in the last day and a half, 'Why did you choose Saskatchewan?'" Bibic told the crowd. "For me the answer was simple: it's because Saskatchewan is a great place to invest."
Moe compared the data centre to the construction of the railway across Canada to protect the nation's sovereignty. He stressed the need to protect the data of Canadians.

"Today, the infrastructure has changed, but the purpose has not," Moe said. "That same nation-building purpose calls for a new kind of infrastructure, infrastructure that protects our data and secures our sovereignty."

A news release from the province says the expansion could create as many as 500 permanent jobs, including about 100 management positions, and another 3,000 jobs in areas like security and maintenance.
Carney called the investment a "fantastic example" of the type of project his government is trying to facilitate.
The announcement was attended by former prime ministers Jean Chretien and Stephen Harper, who joined Bibic and Moe on stage for photos.
The provincial government did not immediately reply to a question about whether the expansion would require further approval from the Rural Municipality of Sherwood, where the data centre is located.
The RM and Reeve Ray Orb also did not immediately reply to a message seeking their comment on the expansion.

The RM approved the data centre in April after the province appointed four new council members following resignations. About 100 protesters gathered outside the RM office as the mostly appointed council approved the centre.

items: RM of Sherwood council approves Bell Canada AI data centre near Regina
Saskatoon chamber applauds 'prudent' study, moratorium on data centres

blocks.text: Bibic said he met with Moe and Minister Jeremy Harrison in July to discuss an expansion of the project. The news release says Bell Canada must supply its own power for the expansion, as it had to for the original project.
The two-day summit in Toronto is aimed at attracting $1 trillion in investment amid a turbulent trade war with the United States.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Phil Tank is an award-winning journalist based in Saskatoon. He can be reached at phil.tank@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Raptors, Clippers agree to complete trade to send Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto: reports
articles.summary: The Raptors and Los Angeles Clippers have agreed to complete a trade to send star forward Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto, according to multiple media reports.

image.caption: Kawhi Leonard is seen as a member of the Los Angeles Clippers during a game in March. Per multiple reports, the veteran superstar is finally returning to the Toronto Raptors after the proposed trade between the two franchises can be completed following the league's investigation into the Clippers' a

blocks.text: NBA·New
The Raptors and Los Angeles Clippers have agreed to complete a trade to send star forward Kawhi Leonard back to Toronto, according to multiple media reports.
Deal involving Ingram, Dick, 5 picks has been paused during NBA's cap probe
Reports say the trade will be made official pending a trade call. Shams Charania of ESPN was the first to report the agreement.
The Raptors offered no comment on the reported trade Monday.
CBC Sports has not independently confirmed the reports.
The deal would see L.A. get all-star forward Brandon Ingram, guard Gradey Dick, unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033, a 2027 first-round pick swap and two second-round picks in return.
The deal had been on hold while the NBA investigated Leonard and the Clippers for salary-cap circumvention.
The league completed its investigation on Sept. 2, fining Leonard $700,000 US but declining to suspend him or void his contract.

Although the deal had not been officially submitted to the league while the investigation was underway, Leonard, Ingram and Dick tried to participate with their new teams as much as NBA rules allowed.

Leonard sat in the front row at Kyle Lowry's July 7 news conference at OVO Athletic Centre, where Lowry announced he would retire as a member of the Raptors. Ingram attended a Clippers summer league game in Las Vegas on July 10.

items: Leonard focused on Raptors return with 'clean slate' after avoiding suspension in NBA cap probe

blocks.text: The 35-year-old Leonard averaged 27.9 points, 6.3 rebounds, 3.6 assists, 1.9 steals and 0.4 blocks per game last season for the Clippers in 2025-26.

Ingram averaged 21.5 points, 5.6 rebounds and 3.7 assists in his one season in Toronto, but was injured 11 minutes into Game 5 of the Raptors' first-round playoff series against the Cleveland Cavaliers. He underwent right heel surgery on May 8.
Dick took a step back in his third NBA season, averaging 14 minutes per game in 2025-26, averaging six points, 1.9 rebounds and 0.7 assists, all career lows.
Leonard was the central player in the Raptors' 2019 championship run, but spent just one season with the club before joining his hometown Clippers as a free agent.
Once the trade is completed, Leonard is expected to speak to reporters at the Raptors' media day on Sept. 28.

articles.title: Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding celebration partially funded by Russian oligarch, couple confirms
articles.summary: Donald Trump Jr.'s new wife, Bettina, is confirming that her May wedding weekend celebration was partially funded by a man with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

image.caption: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina have confirmed that their wedding celebrations were partially funded by a Russian oligarch. (Yves Herman/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Donald Trump Jr.'s new wife, Bettina, is confirming that her May wedding weekend celebration was partially funded by a man with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Bettina Trump called Umar Kremlev a 'dear friend' who 'very generously hosted 2 nights of celebration

In a post on her Instagram page Monday morning signed by the couple, Bettina Trump wrote that the man, Umar Kremlev, was a "dear friend," who "very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding."
"It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," it went on.

ProPublica, a nonprofit investigative website, reported earlier Monday that the wedding between Trump Jr. and socialite Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas was heavily funded by Kremlev, a Russian oligarch who heads the International Boxing Association. ProPublica reported that Kremlev "footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars of wedding expenses," including paying to rent out one of two private islands where the three-day party was held and a fireworks show.
In the post, Bettina Trump said that she and the president's son were married in a private ceremony "surrounded ONLY by our family.

"The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds," it went on.

"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."
Kremlev honoured by Putin
That gift comes as Russia remains at war following its invasion of Ukraine and as the president has failed to broker a promised peace deal between the nations.

Kremlev was recently honoured with the Order of Friendship by Putin, according to the International Boxing Association, and accompanied Putin to China as part of a Russian delegation, according to the Chinese state media cited by the outlet.

Trump Jr. has previously been scrutinized over his Russian ties. During the 2016 campaign, his meeting with Russian attorney Natalia Veselnitskaya in Trump Tower was the subject of intense scrutiny by federal and congressional investigators probing whether the Trump campaign co-ordinated with Russia to meddle in the election.

The meeting had been billed as an opportunity to discuss potentially incriminating information about the president's then-Democrat opponent, Hillary Rodham Clinton, as part of the Russian government's efforts to help Trump Jr.'s father win the White House.

articles.title: Violence, fraud mar BARMM elections on a ‘lesser scale’
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — At least four people died while 20 others were injured in shooting and other violent incidents as the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — At least four people died while 20 others were injured in shooting and other violent incidents as the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) finally held its first parliamentary elections on Monday.

While the combined 20,000-strong military and police deployment significantly reduced tensions and made the polls more peaceful than previous ones, several cases of violent incidents, mostly in Cotabato City, still marred the historic event.

At 11:45 p.m. on Sunday, hours before poll centers opened at 5 a.m., three people were killed and 15 others were wounded in a shooting in front of Datu Usman Mampen Elementary School in Barangay Bagua 2 here.
Cotabato police chief Jibin Bongcayao said in a wire report that the shooting happened as members of rival political factions jostled for the right to cast their votes first.
“It started as a struggle for position in the queue between two groups,” Bongcayao said. “It led to shoving, escalated into a fistfight, and eventually, gunfire broke out in a crowded area.”

Another shooting occurred nearly two hours after voting started Monday inside Cotabato City Central Pilot Elementary School along Sinsuat Avenue in Poblacion 6. Four people were hurt and one of them later died. Among those injured was Patrolman Justeen Reo Ga, assigned to the Dinagat Islands provincial police office.

At around noon, tension erupted at Sero Central Elementary School in this city, as government forces confronted unidentified men wielding sticks and steel rods who had destroyed two luxury vehicles outside the school being used as a voting center.
Later in the afternoon, a powerful explosive went off in another school in this city’s downtown area, wounding one person.
Col. Allen Rae Co, Philippine National Police public information chief, told reporters at Camp Crame in Quezon City that the injured individual was the one carrying the improvised explosive device.
“He’s being treated at the hospital as of now. He’s stable. We’re waiting to be able to question him,” Co added.
‘Deeply alarming’
Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua condemned the series of violent incidents, describing them as “deeply alarming.”
The incidents prompted the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to place Cotabato City under its direct control.
Despite this, Co said the BARMM elections have been “generally peaceful” so far.
“In the majority of areas in BARMM, the electoral process has been peaceful. It just so happened that there are incidents like these. We are calibrating our response,” he said.

Alleged cases of election fraud were also recorded in some areas in the region. Maluso town in Basilan was also placed under Comelec control after it was discovered that the ballots for 36 out of 68 precincts had been preshaded.
Comelec Chair George Erwin Garcia said that voting had been halted in the affected precincts with 16,563 voters, adding that the culprit behind the shaded ballots was already identified.
New ballots arriving

He told reporters that voting may be extended up to Tuesday as they wait for freshly printed ballots to arrive in Zamboanga from the National Printing Office in Quezon City. From there, the new ballots will be flown to Basilan in a helicopter.

Voters in Lantawan town, meanwhile, complained to Basilan Gov. Mujiv Hataman they were not able to vote as the precincts where they were listed ran out of ballots. Hataman shared on social media that over 300 voters were disenfranchised as a result.
In Marantao, Lanao del Sur, Mindanao State University professor Tirmizy Abdullah also reported alleged electoral irregularities experienced by his own family.

“Although I was able to cast my vote, I cannot help but feel deeply frustrated and concerned because some of my close relatives were not able to exercise their right to vote,” Abdullah told the Inquirer.
When his relatives arrived at their precincts, they were barred from voting because their names on the master list had already been signed by someone else, he added.

At a press briefing in Makati City, Ana Singson, the spokesperson for election watchdog Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV), said one of their volunteers at Central Oring Elementary School in Buldon, Maguindanao del Norte, flagged several voters for voting multiple times.

blocks.caption: GETTING COUNTED First-time voter Almira Kamin shows her inked finger after casting her ballot at Malingao Elementary School at Kadayangan in the Special Geographic Area of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Mindanao on Monday. Kamin says the historic exercise gives young people like her a chance…

blocks.text: “They are voting on behalf of people who cannot vote or were unable to show up at the precinct,” Singson told reporters, adding:
“They are also handing out sample ballots to support their candidates.”

Another PPCRV volunteer, according to Singson, said the wife of a mayor reportedly ordered some people at Barurao Central Elementary School in Maguindanao del Sur to use the names of those who had yet to vote.

“They said people [identified with] the mayor’s wife came in and took the voters list. They said that all those who have not voted yet, their names are being taken so they can vote for their candidate,” she added.
Singson did not identify the mayor to protect their volunteers.
Voting disruptions also happened in parts of the Special Geographic Area (SGA).
At Nabundas Elementary School in Barangay Nabundas of Malidagao town, SGA, an Inquirer correspondent at the site heard a blast believed to be from a grenade around 11:25 a.m.
Almost at the same time, a clash between police and an armed group erupted in Shariff Saydona Mustapha, halting polling at the same school.
Gino Ballesteros, Shariff Saydona Mustapha Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office head, said sporadic gunshots could still be heard as of 3 p.m.
Voting in Lanao del Sur was generally peaceful, Rep. Ziaur-Rahman “Zia” Adiong said, adding that he was pleased with the turnout.
“This will be the foundation of the regular BARMM government, which will enable it to exercise its true autonomy,” he said.

The Bangsamoro region’s historic parliamentary voting completes the political track of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, the peace deal signed by the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in 2014 after 17 years of peace negotiations.
MILF chair Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim was hopeful the winners would truly serve the Bangsamoro.

There are 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament. The region comprises five provinces, three cities and 63 villages with nearly 2.4 million voters. Election officials said they expected an 80-percent turnout after polling was postponed for several years.

The region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, will be elected by parliament in its first session. —Reports from Edwin Fernandez, Drema Quitayen Bravo, Taher Solaiman, Cong Corrales, Divina Suson, Leah Agonoy, Richel Umel, Amiel Cagayan, Dianne Sampang, Jason Sigales, Mary Joy Salcedo, Luisa Cabato, and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Legendary costume designer Bob Mackie dies aged 87
articles.summary: The "Sultan of Sequins" created iconic and dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John.

blocks.text: Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.
The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.
"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.
The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.
The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.

"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.
Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".
"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.
Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.

Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.

"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."

Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."
"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."
Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.

He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 11m agoAndrew Hastie says Pauline Hanson hasn’t ‘had the courage’ to front media
12m agoChris Bowen downplays reintroduction of fuel excise relief amid renewed surge in oil prices

blocks.caption: Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy
‘Multiculturalism is who we are’: Anne Aly

Multicultural affairs minister Anne Aly was also on the ABC’s National Forum panel. She said Labor was committed to bringing immigration numbers down in a “manageable way” while ensuring the system both met the needs of Australia and was “fair for those who come here”.
She pushed back at claims immigrants were harming social cohesion, pointing to an Australia she grew up in where “nobody cared what language your mum spoke”.

double quotation markThat’s the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we’re losing … Every time we talk about immigration, multiculturalism, it comes from a deficit point of view. Social cohesion becomes the burden of people from different countries who have come here and it is their fault, it is their responsibility to socially cohere. The fact is that multiculturalism is who we are. It is part of our identity. It’s who we are as Australia.
Andrew Hastie says Pauline Hanson hasn’t ‘had the courage’ to front media
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has questioned why Pauline Hanson announced One Nation’s immigration policy via a prerecorded video on social media instead of fronting the media.
Appearing alongside Barnaby Joyce on the ABC’s National Forum, he said he backed parts of One Nation’s immigration plan but was concerned about the lack of detail and Hanson’s silence:

double quotation markWe haven’t seen her at all today. And this is someone who wants to be the prime minister of Australia. And she hasn’t had the courage to front the media today and explain the budgetary, the economic and the human impact of these policy changes that she’s suggesting.

His ongoing battle with One Nation appeared to be tempered, however, with him and Joyce largely exchanging niceties, including Joyce claiming in jest, at one point, that they were “back in bed together”.
Chris Bowen downplays reintroduction of fuel excise relief amid renewed surge in oil prices
Chris Bowen has watered down any expectations that a renewed rise in oil prices will lead to the reintroduction of the federal government’s fuel excise relief.

He said Labor was continuing to look “very closely” at the spike, which was prompted after a series of drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. But he said the federal government had been “very clear” that cutting the fuel excise was a temporary measure.
Bowen said:

double quotation markIt’s not the only cost of living measure that we put in place … At the same time, I’m very much focused on ensuring our ongoing fuel supply in this very difficult international circumstance … We’re not going to respond to every daily movement on the world oil price.
Bowen said the situation in the Middle East was “deeply concerning” and confirmed he would be travelling to Saudi Arabia next week to meet with his counterpart, Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud.

He was also asked about the appointment of the former opposition leader Sussan Ley to the board of Snowy Hydro, given the Coalition abandoned its commitment to net zero under her leadership and she had blamed Labor’s renewable energy rollout on high energy prices.
Bowen said when he saw an Australian who was “well credentialled, I don’t care how they vote”, and described her as a person of “talent and ability”.
Albanese speaks with King Charles

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
Anthony Albanese spoke to King Charles last night, the prime minister revealed.
Albanese last saw the monarch during a visit to Britain in September last year.
“A privilege to speak with His Majesty King Charles III this evening,” Albanese wrote on social media.
“His affection for the Australian people remains strong. I extended Australia’s best wishes to His Majesty and the Royal Family.”

articles.title: Music festival apologizes after Flo Rida uses alcohol props at sober event in Thunder Bay, Ont.
articles.summary: The Wake the Giant Music Festival is facing backlash after headliner Flo Rida, an American rapper, used alcohol props on stage at the sober event in Thunder Bay on Saturday. The annual event aims to…

image.caption: The Wake the Giant Music Festival is facing backlash after Grammy-nominated headliner Flo Rida used alcohol props on stage at the sober event in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Saturday. (Nicky Shaw/CBC)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·New

The Wake the Giant Music Festival is facing backlash after headliner Flo Rida, an American rapper, used alcohol props on stage at the sober event in Thunder Bay on Saturday. The annual event aims to create a safe, inclusive environment for hundreds of Indigenous youth from remote northern communities who attend school in the northwestern Ontario city.
American rapper's performance was 'really heavy and very triggering for a lot of people,' resident says
The Wake the Giant Music Festival is facing backlash after Grammy-nominated headliner Flo Rida used alcohol props on stage at the sober event in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Saturday.

The annual festival, which was launched in 2019, raises awareness to create a safe, inclusive environment for hundreds of Indigenous youth from remote northern communities who attend school in the city.
CBC Thunder Bay reached out to the Wake the Giant Musical Festival for comment, and was referred to a statement it released on social media on Sunday.
The statement said the festival's team apologizes and acknowledges the harm done by the American rapper's performance.
“The props used were not approved by organizers and we clearly communicated to the artist’s team that this was a sober event and that alcohol is not permitted on our stage,” the statement said.

The team also said it shared in the “hurt and disappointment” that many people felt, and wanted to assure the public that this performance does not align with the values of Wake the Giant or the Northern Nishnawbe Education Council, an Indigenous-run education authority.

“We take responsibility for booking the artist and we will take the lessons learned from this experience to ensure our core values will be at the forefront in choosing artists in the future,” the statement said.
Superior Morning8:27Sarah Law: Wake The Giant 2026 Recap
Other performers at the festival included the American group the Wallflowers, featuring Jakob Dylan, Bob Dylan's son, and Tia Wood, a Cree and Salish pop singer-songwriter from Canada.
A ‘very shocking’ performance

Esther Maud, a city resident who was in the VIP section during the performance, attended to show her support for the event, and for her son and his youth drum group, Charging Thunder, which opened the event.
Maud said it might have helped if she had relistened to his music to reflect on what it means and whether she should support it.

“I just went in thinking and being excited that I get to see someone in person that I kind of grew up listening to. So it didn’t even dawn on me what he represents, and what he sings and puts into his music at all."

items: Thunder Bay’s Wake the Giant Music Festival shares stories of culture, healing

blocks.text: Maud said she's going into six years of sobriety from alcohol. She said her mind was blown the moment she saw the first alcohol bottle on the stage during the show, in a space she has grown to love because it’s an alcohol- and drug-free event, and more bottles kept coming.
She could only think about people who are in early recovery or not as strong, and children thinking about what’s going on and if it was normal behaviour, Maud said.
Shortly after Flo Rida performed his third song, Maud left with her family and a friend.

If she were an organizer of the event, she said, “I probably would have put out the message to maybe the security and asked them to come and help us — tell them that we need to remove the bottles off the stage or ... get somebody to maybe do a little pause, and then quickly regroup and let him know that this is not the place for that."
Maud said she appreciated the music festival's efforts in the wake of Flo Rida's controversial performance, and understood they had communicated to him what the event is about.
But she said the apology could have been better, as the performance was “really heavy and very triggering for a lot of people.”

items: Canada’s indifference to the deaths of seven First Nations teenagers is ‘just plain racism’: Tanya Talaga

blocks.text: Maud said she isn't angry at the festival itself and hopes what happened serves as a learning experience.
“I’m disappointed. I’m upset that this happened, but at the same time, I don’t want this one event and this performer to ruin everything else that they work so hard to do."
Organizers still have a chance to continue this work, she said, noting that she still wants to support them no matter what, as she sees their vision and knows how important it is.
“There are so many purposes and reasons to why this festival still needs to go and keep the momentum for the youth."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Nicky Shaw is a reporter for CBC Thunder Bay. She graduated with a Bachelor of Journalism and a minor in Environmental and Climate Humanities from Carleton University. Aligning with her passion for covering global environmental and humanitarian issues, she has worked to develop in-depth multimedia content that shares the diverse experiences of people in Northwestern Ontario.

articles.title: Former Saskatoon private school admin, pictured with paddle in 1997, testifies at former principal's trial
articles.summary: Lou Brunelle, the first defence witness at Duff Friesen's assault trial, said paddling was school policy and parents signed off.

image.caption: Lou Brunelle, then an administrator at Christian Centre Academy, photographed with a wooden paddle for a 1997 Maclean's magazine article. A copy of the photo was entered as an defence exhibit in the assault trial of Duff Friesen on Monday. (Maclean's)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Lou Brunelle, the first defence witness at Duff Friesen's assault trial, said paddling was school policy and parents signed off.
1997 magazine photo now a court exhibit at Duff Friesen's assault trial

A photo of a former administrator for a Saskatoon private Christian school holding a wooden paddle, published in Maclean's magazine 30 years ago, is now evidence in the assault trial of a former principal at the school.
Duff Arthur Friesen faces five counts of assault with a weapon. He has pleaded not guilty to all of them.
Friesen is accused of hitting students with a wooden paddle. The charges stem from his time at Christian Centre Academy from 1997 to 2007.
The school was later renamed Legacy Christian Academy, then Valour Academy. It's closely associated with Mile Two Church, now called Encounter Church.
Lou Brunelle, the man in the magazine photo from 1997, was the first defence witness at the trial. He testified Monday that paddling was school policy and parents signed off.

Brunelle worked at the school from 1989 to 2001, first as a supervisor and then an administrative assistant, reporting to the director and senior to the teachers. He said the role can be compared to that of a vice-principal.
He said the paddle was one of multiple methods, alongside things like demerits and detentions, that the school used to enforce discipline for things like stealing, lying or cheating.
“We would chat with the child. If warranted — three swats,” he told the jury.
He said the student and the discipliner would then pray together.

items: Former student tells jury principal struck him at private Christian School in Saskatoon

blocks.text: Brunelle also testified that none of the staff at the school at the time were certified to work as teachers. He added that the curriculum was approved and that students received Ministry of Education transcripts that allowed them to go on to university.
Crown witnesses
The Crown closed its case Friday after calling five former students, each of whom testified about being struck with a wooden paddle.
Robyn Mandell said Friesen spanked her hard enough to leave bruises for days. She said it was extremely "humiliating, shameful and terrifying."

items: Trial begins for former principal of Sask. private Christian school facing assault charges

blocks.text: Coy Nolin, who testified on Wednesday, told the jury he was called to Friesen's office during a school day after Friesen sent a letter to his mother about his schoolwork, and was told he would be taken off the basketball team if he didn't catch up.
He said Friesen told him he’d be getting paddled and sent back to class. Nolin said he then put his hands on the seat of a chair and bent over.
“He struck me three times,” Nolin said.
The trial is set for two weeks, with Justice Daryl Labach presiding.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aishwarya Dudha is a reporter for CBC Saskatchewan based in Saskatoon. She specializes in immigration, justice and cultural issues and elevating voices of vulnerable people. She has previously worked for CBC News Network and Global News. You can email her at aishwarya.dudha@cbc.ca

articles.title: Amendment to bill in Lords could test legality of £72m Reform donations
articles.summary:
Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements

Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s…
articles.byline: Pippa Crerar, Jessica Elgot and Kiran Stacey

blocks.text: Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced.

In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt.

Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party.

Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons.

Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status.
The extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election.

However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill.
The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year.

Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028.

Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June.

“Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.”

blocks.caption: Lady Taylor told peers that the government was considering how it could strengthen the residency requirements of political donors. Photograph: HoL

blocks.text: Sharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions.
“We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added.
Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour.
“How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said.
“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.”

Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations.

The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.

Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.
Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”.

However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day.

In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.”

The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality.
Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps.
“The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said.
“But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?”
MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament.
They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval.

Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said.

Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”.

articles.title: Protesters voice concern over privatization as Carney's investment summit kicks off
articles.summary: Hundreds of activists gathered in downtown Toronto on Monday to protest against an investment summit organized by Prime Minister Mark Carney.

image.caption: The Canada Investment Summit on Sept. 14-15 is pitching Canada as a safe place for investment at a time of economic uncertainty, but some worry everyday Canadians won't see the benefits. (Michael Cole/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·Updated
Hundreds of activists gathered in downtown Toronto on Monday to protest against an investment summit organized by Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Activists gathered outside city hall as Mark Carney hosts over 100 potential investors Monday

The Canada Investment Summit takes place on Monday and Tuesday in Toronto and is hosted by Carney, who has invited over 100 of the world's largest investors from around the world in the hopes of securing $1 trillion in investments in some 167 projects across the country over the next five years.

At the summit, the prime minister is expected to pitch Canada as a safe and reliable place for investment at a time of economic uncertainty, but some aren't sold on outside investment yielding positive results for everyday Canadians.

Protesters, including representatives of labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates, say they reject the idea of leaving Canada's economic future in the hands of CEOs and worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

On Monday evening, protesters gathered first in Nathan Phillips Square, then marched to a police barrier near the Art Gallery of Ontario, where the summit's opening gala that is closed to the public and the media is being held.

Rachel Small, an organizer with World Beyond War, a non-profit that campaigns against conflict, said Canadians are struggling to afford rent and the cost of living, and need more investment in education, transit and health care.
"Carney is doing the opposite of that," she said.
"He is selling our public resources without any guaranteed returns and at the same time growing industries that will push the world towards greater war and climate catastrophe."

items: Carney is seeking $1 trillion in investments. What will it take to land major deals at this week's summit?

blocks.text: "These billionaires make decisions behind closed doors in our city to decide our futures. Our future is not for sale," Small said.
Monday's assembly of speakers gathered under the banner "The Many vs. The Money," arguing the summit is designed to "auction off" Canadian public resources, according to its website.
What is the Canada Investment Summit? Inside Carney's investment summit in Toronto
National sovereignty and the impact of various projects on the environment was also a prominent concern throughout the speeches.
"Everybody worries about their own backyard. Our front yard is this entire planet and we must stand together to protect it." said Wet’suwet’en Nation Hereditary Chief Na'Moks.
"They're taking everything we survive on and are willing to sell it to foreign investors."
CBC Toronto has reached out to Environment and Climate Change Canada for comment.

items: NDP's Avi Lewis says Carney is selling Canadian assets to 'the captains of Wall Street'

blocks.text: Speaker Nik Barry-Shaw, trade and privatization campaigner for the Council of Canadians, which advocates for clean water, green energy and fair trade, referenced the prime minister's speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in January when he said: "If we're not at the table, we're on the menu."
"I've been looking around the table that Carney has set for this summer and I don't see any of us at the table," he said. "Does that mean we're on the menu?"

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in a statement Sunday that he welcomes foreign investment, noting 15 major projects in the province "worth tens of billions of dollars" are set to be discussed. They range from mining to energy production and AI.
"We are building an economy that can compete with anyone, anywhere," he said in the statement. "That’s going to be my message throughout the Canada Investment Summit."
"Ontario has what the world needs and we’re going to make sure the world knows it."
Concerns over foreign investment not new: expert

Jeff Mahon, director for geopolitical and international business at consulting firm StrategyCorp., told CBC Radio's Metro Morning that concerns over foreign investment are not new, and pointed to Canada's Investment Canada Act, which reviews deals for their net benefit and impact on jobs and economic competitiveness.

"Foreign investment is really important for the Canadian economy, but there's always going to be some considerations on whether the owner or type of investment will lead to some challenges down the line," he said.

items: From pipelines to railways and AI: Ottawa pitches 167 projects ahead of Carney's investment summit
Carney's pitch to unlock trillions in global investment

blocks.text: Mahon said Canada's trade war with the U.S. is "definitely" a catalyst for the initiative, and understands the push to drive more outside funding.

"When the U.S. shuts down market access or threatens market access, that undermines investment confidence in Canada," he said. "If we don't have investment coming in then that means future economic activity is inhibited, it's going to be undermined."
"Those investment dollars lead to productive investment … that means future economic growth could be higher."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Amy van den Berg is a writer and editor based in Toronto. She often writes about human interest stories, travel and design and her work has appeared in CBC, Monocle, The Walrus, and Toronto Life.
With files from Abby Hughes and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Arctic power plays: EU searches for a new strategy
articles.summary: Russia’s aggression, Trump’s threats against Greenland and the race for critical raw materials are pushing the Arctic to the top of Europe’s agenda.

image.caption: Looking ahead: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders gathered in Finland to discuss the future of the ArcticImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia’s war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention.
"There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition."
The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest."
A changing security environment in the High North

The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North.
"We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said.

The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and… uses its presence for hybrid activities every day."
Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials.

blocks.caption: European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as wellImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Confrontation replaces cooperation
"From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland.

For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe.

The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies.
Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities.

"But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW.
The United States as an additional stress factor

The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies.

"Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland, these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation."
Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkila believes the region is increasingly divided.
"In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW.
He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights.
"Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkila.
Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis
Climate change is transforming the Arctic

At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova.
Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners.

"Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said.

He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change."
Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience'
At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience.
"We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said.

Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown.
